title: End‑to‑End 4‑Bit Training
summary: Training large language models involves calculating and storing a lot of numbers. Using fewer bits for each value reduces memory usage and allows GPUs to perform calculations faster. However, there is a tradeoff: fewer bits also mean fewer representable numbers, leading to more aggressive rounding. Lower-precision representations ultimately hurt accuracy by adding error to the calculations. For example, suppose we want to store the number 3.2, but the nearest values our numerical format can represent are 3 and 4. Rounding to 3 introduces a quantization error of −0.2-0.2−0.2, the difference between the actual value and the one that can be represented in the quantized format. A single error like this may seem small, but these errors accumulate over training as rounding happens repeatedly across layers and optimization steps, which can impair the learning process.

title: Providing Accuracy Guarantees for the Fixed-Point Emulation of Matrix Multiplication
summary: Providing Accuracy Guarantees for the Fixed-Point Emulation of Matrix Multiplication Fixed-point methods such as Ozaki-II emulate double-precision matrix multiplication (GEMM) on fast low-precision hardware. Software that chooses the mantissa bit count automatically is numerically safe when the emulated product keeps the error guarantee of the floating-point GEMM it replaces. We analyze the worst-case and average-case error of fixed-point and floating-point dot products, define exponent span capacities that determine the extra mantissa bits an input requires, and approximate them with a low-precision GEMM. We prove that 53 bits plus such a capacity and a small constant preserve the classical worst-case error bound for a floating-point dot product, and we demonstrate this guarantee in software on several test cases. In a developer build of cuBLAS on an NVIDIA B200, each implemented bit-count rule earns grade~A on Test~2c of ``Grading the BLAS’' at every size and exponent range tested, falling back to double precision at the widest ranges; in exact arithmetic, the bound holds on every adversarial and random input tested. nhorrocks@nvidia.com Fri, 11/13/2026 - 15:41

title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
summary: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page. Tags: leaflet , datasette , openstreetmap
